2-Year Auction Sees Foreign Bid Ease but Record Domestic Demand

The first of this week’s three coupon (>1 year in maturity) Treasury auctions came today in $69 billion of 2-year notes, and while the end result was a bit soft, the mix of buyers stood out. Direct (domestic) bidders ended up with a record share after indirect bidders, a group that includes foreign buyers, fell to the lowest since November 2021.

The sale cleared at 4.708%, down from 4.787% in September, which was the highest since May 2024, and tailed (came in above expectations) by +0.3bps against a when-issued of 4.705%. That was the second straight tail, after +0.2bps in September, and compares with a 6-mth avg of a -0.2bps stop-through.

Looking at the rest of the metrics:

-Overall demand (bid/cover) fell to 2.59, the lowest since March, from 2.63 in September and below the 6-mth avg of 2.64.

-Indirect bidders (which include foreign buyers) dropped to 45.7%, the lowest since November 2021, from 57.8% in September and well below the six-month average of 58.3%.

-Direct (domestic) bidders jumped to 41.3%, the highest in Treasury data going back to 2008 (easily topping 38.2% in October 2012), from 29.0% in September and well above the six-month average of 30.4%.

-That left dealers (another metric of the strength of demand - the lower the better) with 13.0%, down from 13.2% in September but above the six-month average of 11.3%.

The indirect drop is worth watching and comes on the heels of my post this weekend about concerns that Japanese investors may be stepping back from Treasuries (link below). Indirect bidders also include US funds, though, so Treasury’s investor-class data for October, released with a lag, will show how much of the pullback was actually foreign.

@investingLive’s Greg Michalowski gave it a C−, calling it “a soft auction, although the small tail and modest miss in bid to cover keep it from being a particularly poor result he said.

Also catching headlines this morning: Bloomberg picked up a Gartner analysis from earlier this month showing a yawning gap between its forecasts for AI spending and AI revenue.

Gartner expects AI providers to spend nearly $1 trillion on AI infrastructure this year and another $6 trillion from 2027 through 2030. Covering that spending, plus financing costs and a 12% return on invested capital, would take a cumulative $8.5 trillion in revenue through 2030.

Gartner forecasts no more than $3.6 trillion in enterprise and consumer AI revenue attributable to those data centers, about 42% of what’s needed. That leaves a roughly $4.9 trillion revenue gap, and more than $3.5 trillion of AI infrastructure spending exposed to impairment by the end of 2030, rising to more than $4 trillion through 2032. Gartner doesn’t expect that 12% return to be reached until the end of 2032 at the earliest.

The cloud math is no kinder. Gartner sees spending on AI-optimized infrastructure-as-a-service (IaaS) growing from $66 billion in 2027 to $174 billion in 2030. “The growth in spending on AI-optimized IaaS will be too low for most AI compute providers to recover their AI investments before the current generation of AI semiconductors is replaced,” said Gartner analyst Will Sommer. By my math, even that 2030 figure is only about 12% of the roughly $1.5 trillion a year Gartner expects AI providers to spend on infrastructure from 2027 through 2030.

Neoclouds are the most exposed. As Gartner notes, Microsoft ($MSFT), Alphabet ($GOOGL) and Amazon ($AMZN) have diversified revenue that could sustain AI spending for years, while specialists like CoreWeave ($CRWV) and Nebius Group ($NBIS) need returns soon.

Gartner predicts more than 80% of neocloud providers will cease independent operations by 2030. “All of them want to be the full-stack. They can’t all be,” Sommer told Bloomberg. “For every dollar that’s spent on compute, only a fraction of that is going to the owners of compute.”

The options market is starting to brace for that. Put open interest in CoreWeave, Nebius and IREN ($IREN) has climbed sharply this year, per Bloomberg.

@C_Barraud’s packed Monday Brief had an interesting pairing of posts: China’s National Team is buying at its fastest pace since the April 2025 tariff rout, but it hasn’t been able to turn around the selloff.

▪️ National Team ETF inflows were ¥128.7B last week, about 92% of the April 2025 peak (Bloomberg)
▪️ The CSI 300 entered a bear market Thursday, 20.2% below its June 22 high and at its lowest since July 2025, after a record 10-week losing streak
▪️ Friday’s 1.7% bounce stalled Monday, with the index finishing little changed

The difference from April 2025 may be that more fundamental issues are behind this selloff:

Looking at the seasonality breakdown for the upcoming week from @AlmanacTrader, editor of the Stock Trader’s Almanac & Almanac Investor Newsletter, the last week of October has historically closed the month on a firm note, and in midterm years Day 21 (Thursday) has been quite strong.

Monday is trading day 18. Over the past 31 years it has been one of the weaker days of the month, with the major indices down about 0.2–0.4%. Tuesday and Thursday have more than made up for it, each adding roughly 0.3–0.5%, while Wednesday has been about flat. Net, the week has gained about 0.5–0.65% for every major index, including the Russell 2000. That has left October up about 1.5–1.9% on average for the large-cap indices and about 0.5% for the Russell 2000.

Midterm years have been stronger again, led by small caps. The Russell 2000 has gained about 1.6%, the Nasdaq about 0.85%, the Russell 1000 about 0.75%, and the Dow and S&P about 0.5%. Some of that gap reflects which years are averaged: the Russell data only start with the 1982 midterm, while the Dow and S&P go back to 1950. The standout is Thursday, the best day of the week for every midterm line, adding about 0.65–0.85%. For the DJIA, S&P and Russell 1000, that one day has matched or exceeded the entire week’s gain. October has finished up about 3–4% in midterm years, compared with 1.5–1.9% for the large caps across all years.

That hands off to November, the start of what the Almanac calls the “Best Six Months” (November–April), and to the midterm election on Tuesday, November 3rd. Historically, midterms have been followed by strength. 

The S&P 500 has been higher one year after all 19 midterm elections since 1950, by about 15% on average according to a Motley Fool count, and by 16.6% according to BNY. Even after 1986, with the October 1987 crash in that window, the S&P finished about 1% higher.

In terms of hyperscaler performance, have we moved past how much capex are they spending to how much free cash flow are they generating?

Despite a robust outlook with Mag-7 earnings expected to climb about 34% this year, above the 29% pace of the S&P 500, according to Bloomberg Intelligence data, and 27% in 2027, a consensus that has moved up aggressively in recent weeks (two months ago, analysts were anticipating an increase of less than 19%), the Bloomberg Magnificent Seven Index is up just 6.5% this year, well below the 11% rise in the S&P 500 Index and the 15% rise in the tech-heavy Nasdaq 100 Index.

“If we get another scenario where we have to lower FCF expectations, that will elevate concerns about the durability of AI spending and the reliance on incremental capital, and that will flow down to the neoclouds and other parts of the market as well,” said Kevin Shea, senior equity analyst at BNY Wealth. “However, if we can get positive revisions to FCF, the market will breathe a sigh of relief that we’ve reached the bottom for negative revisions and that we’re through the most difficult part of the spending cycle.”

So maybe pollsters aren’t irrelevant after all. Despite just an ~20% chance of victory according to Polymarket and Kalshi, President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva came from behind to win Brazil’s presidential runoff on Sunday, taking 51.76% of the vote to 48.24% for Flávio Bolsonaro, per the Financial Times.

The polls though had called it a statistical dead heat. Datafolha’s final survey had the race tied at 50% each, and the average of final polls gave Bolsonaro a narrow 50.9% to 49.1% edge, per Newsweek. That’s well within the margin of error, and a long way from the roughly 4-to-1 odds prediction markets gave Bolsonaro.

It’s also a first. No first-round runner-up had won the presidency since Brazil restored elections in 1989, and Lula turned Bolsonaro’s 2.2 million-vote first-round lead into a 4.4 million-vote margin, per the FT.

Markets aren’t taking it well. The iShares MSCI Brazil ETF (EWZ) is down over 17% in overnight trading. Traders had piled into Brazilian assets on hopes that Bolsonaro would be more committed to cutting spending. Lula has promised a fiscal adjustment without saying how he’ll deliver it, and has made clear he won’t sacrifice his social agenda to satisfy markets. He’ll also face a more hostile Congress after conservative parties made sweeping gains in this month’s congressional elections, per the FT.
